topic: Build & release: Gradle, R8, build variants & modularization

questions.question: You add a new `:feature:search` module folder with its own `build.gradle.kts`, but Gradle ignores it. Which file must you edit?
options: `settings.gradle.kts` (add `include(":feature:search")`)
The root `build.gradle.kts` (add it to `allprojects {}`)
`app/build.gradle.kts` (add it under `android {}`)
`gradle.properties` (add `modules=:feature:search`)
questions.explanation: The settings file defines which projects make up the build (plus plugin and dependency repositories). The root and module build files only configure projects that settings has already included.

questions.question: Android names each variant flavor + BuildType. This plain-Kotlin model builds the variant matrix. What does it print?
options:
4
freeDebug, freeRelease, paidDebug, paidRelease

4
debugFree, releaseFree, debugPaid, releasePaid

2
freeDebug, paidRelease

4
freeDebug, paidDebug, freeRelease, paidRelease
questions.explanation: `flatMap` goes through every flavor and, for each one, every build type, so you get 2 × 2 = 4 combinations with the flavor first. That is also how AGP builds variants: the product flavors times the build types, named like `freeDebug`.

questions.question: Google Play rejects an upload that reuses a `versionCode` already uploaded for that app, even if `versionName` changed.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Play uses the integer `versionCode` to identify builds and decide what counts as an update, so every upload needs a new one, and an update must be higher than the installed version. `versionName` is only a display string, so bumping it alone doesn't help.

questions.question: `:core:network` declares `implementation(libs.okhttp)`. `:feature:home` depends on `:core:network` with `implementation(project(":core:network"))`. What is true?
options: `:feature:home` can't import OkHttp classes, and OkHttp changes don't recompile it
`:feature:home` can import OkHttp classes because dependencies are transitive at compile time
OkHttp is left out of the APK because `:app` doesn't declare it
The build fails because `implementation` dependencies can't be transitive
questions.explanation: `implementation` keeps the dependency off consumers' compile classpath (it is still packaged at runtime), so it doesn't leak and you get compile avoidance. Use `api` only when OkHttp types show up in `:core:network`'s public API.

questions.question: `gradle/libs.versions.toml` contains `androidx-core-ktx = { group = "androidx.core", name = "core-ktx", version.ref = "coreKtx" }`. How do you use it in a module's `build.gradle.kts`?
options: `implementation(libs.androidx.core.ktx)`
`implementation("libs:androidx-core-ktx")`
`implementation(libs["androidx-core-ktx"])`
`implementation(versions.coreKtx)`
questions.explanation: Gradle generates type-safe accessors from the catalog, and the dashes in an alias become dots. Neither the string coordinate form nor a version reference adds the library.

questions.question: Your release build uses R8. Which of these need keep rules (from you or a library) to keep working? Select all that apply.
options: A class loaded with `Class.forName("com.app.plugins.PdfPlugin")`
Fields of a model that Gson fills by reflection from JSON field names
A Kotlin method that native C++ code calls through JNI by name
A private helper function that is only called directly from other Kotlin code
A `sealed` class that is only used in an exhaustive `when`
questions.explanation: R8 can only follow references it can see in bytecode. Names looked up by string through reflection, reflection-based serialization or JNI look unused, so they get removed or renamed. Code that is called directly is traced correctly and needs no rule.

questions.question: A Crashlytics report from your release build shows `at a.b.c(Unknown Source:12)`. What do you need to get a readable stack trace?
options: The `mapping.txt` R8 generated for that exact build, uploaded or used with retrace
The `mapping.txt` from today's build of `main`, since R8 renames classes the same way each time
A debug build installed on the user's device
Turning off obfuscation and asking the user to reproduce it
questions.explanation: R8's renaming changes from build to build, so only the mapping file from the build that crashed can decode it. That's why CI should archive or upload `mapping.txt` for every release.

questions.question: In a release build type you can set `isShrinkResources = true` while leaving `isMinifyEnabled = false`.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The resource shrinker relies on code shrinking to find out which resources are still referenced, so AGP fails the build if you enable resource shrinking without `isMinifyEnabled = true`.

questions.question: An app has `flavorDimensions += listOf("tier", "env")`, flavors `free`/`paid` (tier) and `dev`/`prod` (env), and the build types `debug` and `release`. How many build variants are there?
questions.explanation: The variant count is the product of each dimension's flavors times the build types: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, for example `freeDevDebug` or `paidProdRelease`. Dimensions multiply, they don't add.

questions.question: A team computes `versionCode` from semantic versions. What does this print?
questions.code:
fun code(major: Int, minor: Int, patch: Int) =
    major * 10_000 + minor * 100 + patch

fun main() {
    val codes = listOf(code(1, 9, 0), code(1, 10, 0), code(2, 0, 1))
    println(codes)
    println(codes.zipWithNext().all { (a, b) -> b > a })
    println("1.10.0" > "1.9.0")
}
questions.explanation: The integer formula always grows from 1.9.0 to 1.10.0 to 2.0.1. Comparing the strings `"1.10.0" > "1.9.0"` checks characters one by one, and `'1' < '9'`, so it gives `false`. That's why ordering must use `versionCode`, not `versionName`.

questions.question: Which statements about Android App Bundles (AAB) are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Play generates optimized split APKs from the bundle, so a device downloads only the code and resources for its ABI, screen density and language
New apps published on Google Play must be uploaded as AABs, not APKs
You can't `adb install` an `.aab` directly; `bundletool` (or Play) turns it into installable APKs
Uploading an AAB means you no longer have to increase `versionCode`
An AAB doesn't need to be signed because Play signs it
questions.explanation: An AAB is a publishing format: Play builds and signs split APKs for each device configuration. You still sign the bundle with your upload key, and `versionCode` must still go up.

questions.question: Your app uses Play App Signing and a developer has lost the upload keystore. What happens?
options: Google's app signing key is safe; you request an upload key reset and use the new key
The app can never be updated again and must be published under a new package name
You re-sign with the debug keystore, since Play re-signs every upload with the app signing key anyway
Play generates a new app signing key, so existing users must reinstall
questions.explanation: With Play App Signing, Google keeps the key that signs what users install, and you only sign uploads with an upload key. A lost upload key can be reset, while users keep getting updates signed with the same app signing key.

questions.question: Setting `applicationIdSuffix = ".debug"` on the debug build type lets the debug and release builds be installed side by side on the same device.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The suffix changes the final application ID, for example `com.app.debug`, and Android treats that as a different app. The code's `namespace` (the R and BuildConfig package) stays the same.

questions.question: `:feature:search` needs to open a profile screen that lives in `:feature:profile`. Following the usual modularization rules, what should you do?
options: Expose a callback like `onOpenProfile(id)` from `:feature:search` and let `:app` wire it to the profile route
Add `implementation(project(":feature:profile"))` to `:feature:search`
Make both features depend on each other with `api` so they can share screens
Move the profile screen into `:core:common` so every feature can reach it without depending on another feature
questions.explanation: Feature modules shouldn't depend on each other: that couples them and limits parallel and incremental builds. The `:app` module (or a shared navigation contract) connects them, and core modules shouldn't absorb feature UI.

questions.question: Which statements about Gradle dependency configurations are correct? Select all that apply.
options: `testImplementation` adds a library (e.g. MockK) only to the local unit test source set
`compileOnly` makes a library available when compiling but doesn't package it into the APK
`runtimeOnly` lets your code reference the library's classes at compile time
`api` should be the default choice because it makes dependency graphs simpler
questions.explanation: `runtimeOnly` is the opposite of `compileOnly`: the library is packaged but not visible to the compiler. Defaulting to `api` leaks dependencies to every consumer and makes more modules recompile, so `implementation` is the right default.

questions.question: Twelve Android library modules each repeat the same `compileSdk`, `minSdk`, Kotlin JVM target and lint settings. What is the recommended fix?
options: A convention plugin in an included `build-logic` build, applied by ID in each module
Move the block into `allprojects {}` or `subprojects {}` in the root build file, so it's applied once
Keep copy-pasting, since Gradle caches identical blocks
Put the settings in `gradle.properties` as `android.compileSdk=...`
questions.explanation: Convention plugins keep shared config in one typed, testable place, and each module opts in explicitly. Cross-project configuration through `allprojects`/`subprojects` couples projects and conflicts with project isolation, and `gradle.properties` has no such Android DSL keys.

questions.question: You add `buildConfigField("String", "API_URL", "\"https://dev.api\"")` to the `dev` flavor, but `BuildConfig.API_URL` doesn't resolve. On current AGP, what's the most likely cause?
options: `BuildConfig` isn't generated unless you set `buildFeatures { buildConfig = true }`
`buildConfigField` only works inside build types, so flavor fields are silently dropped
The value must not be wrapped in escaped quotes
You must use `resValue` for strings instead
questions.explanation: Recent AGP versions don't generate `BuildConfig` unless you opt in with `buildFeatures.buildConfig`. `buildConfigField` works in flavors and build types, and String values do need the inner escaped quotes because they're pasted into Java source.

questions.question: A large multi-module project has slow builds. Which changes usually make them faster? Select all that apply.
options: Turning on the Gradle configuration cache so the configuration phase can be reused
Migrating Room/Hilt annotation processing from kapt to KSP
Switching `api` to `implementation` where a dependency's types aren't exposed
Turning on `isMinifyEnabled` for the debug build type
Making every feature depend on one big `:core` module through `api`
questions.explanation: The configuration cache skips reconfiguration, KSP avoids kapt's Java stub generation, and `implementation` shrinks recompilation fan-out. R8 in debug adds a slow step, and one large `api` hub makes almost every change recompile everything.

questions.question: Your Android library loads its parser classes by reflection. Apps that use it crash in release builds with `ClassNotFoundException`. What's the correct fix in the library?
options: Ship the keep rules via `consumerProguardFiles("consumer-rules.pro")` so the app's R8 applies them
Add the rules to the library's own `proguardFiles(...)` in its release build type, so the AAR keeps those classes
Set `isMinifyEnabled = false` in the library module
Tell every app to turn off R8
questions.explanation: Apps usually shrink the library code themselves. Only consumer rules bundled in the AAR reach the app's R8 configuration. The library's own `proguardFiles` apply only when the library itself is minified and aren't passed on to apps.

questions.question: On current AGP versions R8 runs in full mode by default. Full mode is more aggressive than ProGuard-compatible mode, so code that only works through reflection (such as default constructors used by a serializer) can break unless you keep it explicitly.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Full mode became the default and drops some of ProGuard's lenient assumptions, for example implicitly keeping default constructors or attributes for classes that are only kept by name. Reflection-based code often needs more precise keep rules after upgrading.
